mainEntity.name: What is method overriding in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Method overriding in Java is when a subclass provides a specific implementation of a method that is already defined in its parent class. The overriding method must have the same name, same parameter list (signature), and a compatible return type. It enables runtime polymorphism — the JVM decides at runtime which version of the method to call based on the actual object type, not the reference type. Overriding is achieved through inheritance and is the foundation of dynamic method dispatch in Java.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between method overriding and method overloading in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Method overloading is compile-time polymorphism — same method name, different parameter lists, resolved at compile time, can exist in the same class. Method overriding is runtime polymorphism — same method name AND same parameter list, different implementation in subclass, resolved at runtime based on actual object type. Overloading changes the method signature; overriding keeps the exact same signature but changes the body. @Override annotation is used only with overriding, not overloading.

mainEntity.name: What are the rules for method overriding in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: The key rules for method overriding in Java are: (1) The method name and parameter list must be identical to the parent class method. (2) The return type must be the same or a covariant (subtype) of the parent's return type. (3) The access modifier cannot be more restrictive than the parent method — it can be the same or less restrictive. (4) The overriding method cannot throw new or broader checked exceptions than the parent method. (5) Static, final, and private methods cannot be overridden. (6) The method must be inherited — i.e., the class must be a subclass of the class where the method is defined.

mainEntity.name: What is the use of @Override annotation in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: The @Override annotation in Java is a compile-time marker that tells the compiler: 'I intend this method to override a method in the parent class or interface.' If the method does NOT actually override anything (e.g., wrong parameter type, typo in method name), the compiler throws an error, preventing silent bugs. It also improves code readability — any developer can immediately see which methods are overrides. While optional, @Override is strongly recommended for every overriding method as a best practice.

mainEntity.name: Can we override a static method in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: No — static methods cannot be overridden in Java. If a subclass defines a static method with the same signature as a parent's static method, it is called method hiding, not overriding. The key difference: with overriding, the method called depends on the object's actual runtime type (dynamic dispatch). With method hiding, the method called depends on the reference type at compile time (static dispatch). @Override on a static method will cause a compile-time error. Static methods belong to the class, not instances, so polymorphism does not apply.

sections.title: What is Method Overriding in Java?

blocks.text: Method overriding in Java is a feature of object-oriented programming that allows a subclass to provide its own specific implementation of a method already defined in its parent class (superclass). The overriding method in the subclass must have the same name, same parameter list, and a compatible return type as the method in the parent class.

Method overriding is the mechanism that enables runtime polymorphism (also called dynamic polymorphism) in Java. When you call an overridden method on a reference variable, the JVM decides at runtime — based on the actual object type, not the reference type — which version of the method to execute. This is called Dynamic Method Dispatch and is the foundation of flexible, extensible object-oriented design.

Real-world analogy: Consider a general Animal class with a sound() method. A Dog subclass overrides sound() to print "Woof", and a Cat subclass overrides it to print "Meow". When you call sound() on an Animal reference that actually holds a Dog object, Java calls Dog's version — not Animal's. This is overriding in action.

blocks.title: 🔑 Method Overriding at a Glance
blocks.text: Method overriding requires: (1) Inheritance — subclass must extend a superclass. (2) Same method name and parameter list. (3) Compatible (same or covariant) return type. (4) Access modifier not more restrictive than parent. (5) No new or broader checked exceptions. Use @Override annotation always. Enables: runtime polymorphism and dynamic method dispatch. Cannot override: static, final, private methods, or constructors.

To override a method, the subclass defines a method with the exact same signature (name + parameter list) as the parent class method. The @Override annotation above the method signals the intent to the compiler and is strongly recommended.

items.title: Syntax

4. Cannot throw broader checked exceptions.

items.title: How It Works
items.text: Parent reference → Child object → method called → JVM checks actual object type at runtime → executes Child's version. This is Dynamic Method Dispatch. The decision is made at runtime, not compile time.

sections.title: Rules of Method Overriding in Java

blocks.text: Java enforces strict rules for method overriding. Violating any of these rules either results in a compile-time error or causes the method to be treated as a new method (not an override). Knowing these rules thoroughly is essential for both writing correct code and clearing Java interviews.

items.title: Rule 1: Same Method Name & Parameter List
items.text: The overriding method must have the EXACT same name and parameter list (number, type, and order of parameters) as the parent class method. If the parameter list differs even slightly, Java treats it as method OVERLOADING, not overriding — creating a new, separate method. @Override annotation catches this mistake at compile time.

items.title: Rule 2: Compatible Return Type
items.text: The return type must be the same as or a subtype of the parent method's return type (covariant return type — introduced in Java 5). Example: parent returns Animal, child can return Dog (since Dog is a subtype of Animal). Primitive types must match exactly — int cannot be changed to long. void must remain void.

items.title: Rule 3: Access Modifier — Same or Less Restrictive
items.text: The overriding method's access modifier cannot be MORE restrictive than the parent method. Allowed: public → public, protected → protected or public, default (package) → default, protected, or public. NOT allowed: public → protected (more restrictive). This ensures the Liskov Substitution Principle — a subclass must be usable wherever its parent is expected.

items.title: Rule 4: Checked Exception Rules
items.text: The overriding method CANNOT throw new checked exceptions or broader checked exceptions than the parent method. It CAN throw fewer checked exceptions, narrower (subtype) checked exceptions, or any number of unchecked (runtime) exceptions. Example: if parent throws IOException, child cannot throw Exception (broader), but can throw FileNotFoundException (narrower) or remove it entirely.

items.title: Rule 5: Cannot Override static, final, or private Methods
items.text: static methods: cannot be overridden — only hidden (method hiding). final methods: explicitly marked as non-overridable — compile error if attempted. private methods: not visible to subclasses — subclass defines a completely new method, not an override. Constructors: cannot be overridden — they are not inherited.

items.title: Rule 6: Inheritance is Required
items.text: Method overriding REQUIRES an IS-A relationship — the subclass must extend (or implement) the class that defines the original method. Overriding cannot happen within the same class (that would be overloading). The @Override annotation on a method that doesn't override anything (no IS-A relation) causes a compile error.

public final void finalMethod() { System.out.println("Cannot override"); }
private void secretMethod()     { System.out.println("Private — not inherited"); }

blocks.text: The @Override annotation (introduced in Java 5) is placed above a method to explicitly declare the programmer's intent: "this method is overriding a method from the superclass or interface." It is a compile-time annotation — it does not affect runtime behaviour, but it is one of the most important defensive practices in Java OOP.

public String Describe() {   // Capital D — typo!
// result: Shape's describe() is called on Circle objects — silent bug!
// ✅ Bug CAUGHT WITH @Override — compile error immediately
// ERROR: method does not override or implement a method from a supertype

System.out.println(s.describe());                // Output: I am a shape. (bug!)
System.out.println(r.describe());                // Output: I am a rectangle...

blocks.title: 💡 Always Use @Override — Zero Cost, Maximum Safety
blocks.text: @Override has absolutely NO runtime cost — it is stripped by the compiler and never present in bytecode. It provides: (1) Compile-time verification that you actually ARE overriding something. (2) Instant notification if the parent method signature changes — your override will break at compile time, not silently at runtime. (3) Self-documenting code — readers immediately know this method is an override. There is literally no reason not to use it. Make it a strict personal rule: EVERY overriding method gets @Override.

The super keyword in the context of method overriding allows a subclass to explicitly call the overridden parent class method from within the overriding method. This is useful when the child class wants to extend (add to) the parent's behaviour rather than completely replace it. super.methodName() always calls the direct parent's version of the method.

return baseTax + engineTax; // Extend, don't replace

// Electric cars get 50% discount on tax

blocks.title: ⚠️ super.method() Can Only Go One Level Up
blocks.text: super.methodName() always refers to the DIRECT parent class — you cannot skip levels with super.super.methodName(). If ElectricCar calls super.displayInfo(), it calls Car's version (not Vehicle's directly). If Car's version calls super.displayInfo(), it then calls Vehicle's version. This chaining is by design — it enforces the inheritance hierarchy and prevents bypassing intermediate class logic.

sections.title: Covariant Return Type in Method Overriding

blocks.text: Covariant return type (introduced in Java 5) allows the overriding method in a subclass to return a subtype of the return type declared in the parent class method. Before Java 5, the return type had to be exactly the same. Covariant return types make method overriding more flexible and enable cleaner API design — particularly useful in the Builder pattern, factory methods, and fluent APIs.

lines: // ✅ Covariant return type: Dog (subtype of Animal) — valid override
public Dog createAnimal() {   // Returns Dog instead of Animal
// Real-world: Builder pattern using covariant return type
// ✅ Covariant: returns EmployeeBuilder instead of PersonBuilder
// This allows fluent chaining without casting
return this; // Returns EmployeeBuilder, not PersonBuilder
Dog dog = factory.createAnimal(); // No cast needed — returns Dog directly

sections.title: Dynamic Method Dispatch — The Heart of Runtime Polymorphism

blocks.text: Dynamic Method Dispatch (DMD) is the mechanism by which Java resolves overridden method calls at runtime, based on the actual type of the object the reference points to — not the declared type of the reference variable. This is the technical underpinning of runtime polymorphism and is what makes Java's OOP so powerful and flexible.

blocks.label: DynamicMethodDispatch.java
lines: public void draw() { System.out.println("Drawing a Circle (radius=" + radius + ")"); }
public double area() { return Math.PI * radius * radius; }
Rectangle(double w, double h) { this.w = w; this.h = h; }
public void draw() { System.out.println("Drawing a Rectangle (" + w + "x" + h + ")"); }
public double area() { return w * h; }
Triangle(double b, double h) { this.base = b; this.height = h; }
public void draw() { System.out.println("Drawing a Triangle (base=" + base + ")"); }
public double area() { return 0.5 * base * height; }
// JVM decides which draw() and area() to call AT RUNTIME
s.draw();  // Dynamic dispatch — correct draw() called for each
// ✅ Power of DMD: Add new shape without changing this method
s.draw();   // Always calls correct version at runtime

blocks.title: 📌 How JVM Implements Dynamic Dispatch — vtable
blocks.text: Under the hood, the JVM uses a virtual method table (vtable) — a per-class table of method pointers. When a class overrides a method, its vtable entry for that method points to its own version. At runtime, the JVM looks up the object's actual class, finds its vtable, and invokes the correct method. This lookup is O(1) and highly optimized — the JVM's JIT compiler frequently inlines monomorphic call sites (where only one class is ever passed), making polymorphic calls nearly as fast as direct calls.

An abstract method is a method declared with the abstract keyword in an abstract class — it has no body (no implementation). Every non-abstract subclass that extends an abstract class must override all abstract methods, or it must itself be declared abstract. Abstract methods enforce a contract: subclasses must provide their own implementation. This is the most explicit form of method overriding in Java.

blocks.text: When a class implements an interface, it must provide implementations (overrides) for all abstract methods of that interface — unless the class is abstract itself. Java 8 introduced default methods in interfaces — methods with a body. These can optionally be overridden by implementing classes. Java 8 also introduced static interface methods (cannot be overridden) and Java 9 added private interface methods (cannot be overridden).

blocks.title: ⚠️ Default Method Conflict Resolution
blocks.text: When a class implements two interfaces that both define a default method with the same name and signature, the class MUST override that method to resolve the ambiguity — otherwise you get a compile-time error. Inside the overriding method, you can explicitly call either interface's default method using InterfaceName.super.methodName() syntax. If a class also inherits a concrete method from a superclass with the same name, the superclass method wins over interface defaults (class always beats interface).

sections.title: Method Overriding vs Method Overloading — Key Differences

blocks.text: Method overriding and method overloading are both forms of polymorphism in Java but they work differently, serve different purposes, and are resolved at different times. Confusing the two is one of the most common mistakes in Java interviews and production code.

Same class has multiple methods with the same name but different parameters
No — can exist in the same class
Can be different (not part of signature)
Cannot be more restrictive than parent
Provide multiple ways to call the same logical operation
JVM resolves at runtime based on actual object type
Compiler resolves at compile time based on method signature

sections.title: Methods That Cannot Be Overridden in Java

blocks.text: Not all methods in Java can be overridden. Understanding which methods cannot be overridden — and why — is essential for both writing correct code and answering interview questions with confidence.

items.title: final Methods
items.text: A method declared final cannot be overridden in any subclass. Attempting to override it causes a compile-time error. Use final when the method's behaviour must remain constant throughout the inheritance hierarchy — e.g., security-critical logic, template method steps that must not be changed. Example: String.intern(), Object.getClass() are final in Java's standard library.

items.title: static Methods — Method Hiding
items.text: Static methods belong to the class, not instances — they have no runtime polymorphism. If a subclass defines a static method with the same signature, it HIDES the parent's method — this is called method hiding, not overriding. The key difference: which version is called depends on the REFERENCE TYPE (compile-time), not the object type (runtime). @Override on a static method causes a compile error.

items.title: private Methods
items.text: Private methods are not visible outside their class and cannot be inherited. If a subclass defines a method with the same name as a parent's private method, it creates a completely NEW method — not an override. @Override on such a method causes a compile error. There is no runtime or compile-time connection between the parent's private method and the subclass method.

items.title: Constructors
items.text: Constructors are not inherited and therefore cannot be overridden. Each class defines its own constructors. The super() call in a subclass constructor invokes the parent constructor, but that is chaining, not overriding. A method that looks like a constructor but has a return type is actually a regular method — a common beginner confusion.

blocks.label: CannotOverride.java
lines: // ❌ COMPILE ERROR: Cannot override final method
// ℹ️ METHOD HIDING — not overriding; @Override would cause compile error
// ℹ️ NEW method in Child — no relation to Parent's privateMethod()
// Static — resolved by REFERENCE TYPE, not object type (hiding, not overriding)

blocks.text: Java enforces specific rules about what checked exceptions an overriding method can declare. These rules exist to uphold the Liskov Substitution Principle — if you have a reference to the parent class and call a method, you must be able to handle the exceptions declared in the parent. The child class cannot surprise callers with new, broader checked exceptions.

items.title: Allowed: No exception at all
items.text: The overriding method can choose to not throw any checked exception, even if the parent method declared one. This makes the subclass stricter — callers using a child reference don't even need a try-catch for that exception.

items.title: Allowed: Same checked exception
items.text: The overriding method can declare the exact same checked exception as the parent. Callers can handle it identically whether they have a parent or child reference.

items.title: Allowed: Narrower (subtype) checked exception
items.text: The overriding method can declare a subtype of the parent's checked exception. Example: parent throws IOException → child can throw FileNotFoundException (subtype of IOException). Callers handling IOException still catch FileNotFoundException.

items.title: Allowed: Any unchecked (runtime) exception
items.text: The overriding method can throw any unchecked exception (RuntimeException subclasses) regardless of what the parent declares. RuntimeExceptions do not need to be declared or caught — they propagate freely.

items.title: NOT Allowed: New checked exception
items.text: The overriding method CANNOT add a new checked exception not declared in the parent. Example: parent throws IOException → child cannot also throw SQLException. This would break code that only catches IOException when using a parent reference. Compile-time error.

items.title: NOT Allowed: Broader checked exception
items.text: The overriding method CANNOT throw a broader (supertype) checked exception. Example: parent throws FileNotFoundException → child cannot throw IOException (broader). IOException is a supertype of FileNotFoundException — callers handling FileNotFoundException might not catch IOException. Compile-time error.

sections.title: Common Mistakes & Pitfalls — Bugs That Fool Everyone

blocks.text: These mistakes are consistently found in Java code written by developers who understand the concept of overriding but make subtle errors in practice. Each mistake either results in a silent bug (no compile error, wrong runtime behaviour) or a confusing compile error.

blocks.label: CommonMistakes.java
lines: public void print(int x) { System.out.println("Parent: " + x); }
// ❌ MISTAKE 1: Overloading instead of Overriding (different param type)
// This is OVERLOADING (double vs int) — NOT overriding!
// No @Override → no compile error → silent bug: Parent's print(int) still used
public void print(double x) { System.out.println("Child: " + x); }
// ✅ With @Override: compile error immediately reveals the mistake
// public void print(double x) { } // ERROR: method does not override
// Parent's show() is public; cannot reduce to protected
// protected void show() { }  // ERROR: weaker access privileges
// ❌ MISTAKE 3: Calling super after modifying state — unexpected double-action
super.show(); // ✅ Intentional super call is fine
// ❌ But avoid if parent show() has side effects you don't want doubled
// ❌ MISTAKE 4: Forgetting @Override on equals() — silent object comparison bug
// This OVERLOADS equals (Object parameter), not OVERRIDES it!
public boolean equals(StringExample other) {  // ❌ Wrong parameter type
// Object.equals(Object) is still active — old behaviour used in collections!
// ✅ Correct override: parameter must be Object, not StringExample
// ❌ MISTAKE 5: Expecting overriding to work on static methods
class Base  { public static void greet() { System.out.println("Base greet"); } }
class Derived extends Base { public static void greet() { System.out.println("Derived greet"); } }
obj.greet();  // Output: Base greet  ← NOT Derived greet!
// Static methods use reference type (Base), not object type (Derived)
// This is method HIDING, not overriding — no dynamic dispatch

sections.title: Bad Practices & Anti-Patterns — What Senior Developers Reject

blocks.text: These anti-patterns appear in code reviews and cause long-term maintenance problems. Each one represents a misuse or misunderstanding of method overriding that makes code harder to understand, extend, or debug.

items.title: Skipping @Override Annotation
items.text: Never write an overriding method without @Override. Without it, typos in method names or wrong parameter types silently create new methods instead of overrides. The bug only surfaces at runtime — often in production. Rule: EVERY method that intends to override MUST have @Override. Configure your IDE's warning settings to treat missing @Override as an error.

items.title: Completely Ignoring super() in Override
items.text: When overriding, blindly ignoring the parent's implementation can break functionality the parent was maintaining — particularly logging, validation, event firing, lifecycle callbacks. Always evaluate whether super.methodName() should be called. Frameworks (Spring, Android) frequently require super.onCreate(), super.onDestroy(), etc. Skipping them causes subtle, hard-to-diagnose bugs.

items.title: Overriding equals() Without hashCode()
items.text: If you override equals() in a class, you MUST also override hashCode(). Java's contract: equal objects must have the same hash code. Breaking this contract causes objects to behave incorrectly in hash-based collections (HashMap, HashSet, Hashtable) — they won't be found even when they 'should' be equal. This is one of the most dangerous and common OOP mistakes in Java.

items.title: Calling Overridable Methods from Constructor
items.text: If a parent constructor calls a method that the child overrides, the child's version runs while the child's fields are still uninitialized (the child constructor hasn't run yet). This leads to NullPointerException or incorrect state. Rule: never call overridable (non-private, non-final, non-static) methods from constructors. Use factory methods, init() methods, or final methods instead.

items.title: Deep Override Chains Without Documentation
items.text: When overriding methods span 4-5 levels of inheritance hierarchy, understanding what actually runs when you call a method becomes extremely difficult. Each level might call super, modify state, and add behaviour. Document override intentions clearly, keep hierarchies shallow (prefer composition over deep inheritance), and use @Override consistently so the chain is traceable.

items.title: Using instanceof Instead of Polymorphism
items.text: Code like 'if (obj instanceof Dog) { ((Dog) obj).bark(); } else if (obj instanceof Cat) { ((Cat) obj).meow(); }' is a sign that method overriding is not being used where it should be. Define a common sound() method in the parent, override it in each subclass, and call obj.sound() — no instanceof needed. instanceof-based dispatch defeats the entire purpose of polymorphism.

sections.title: Java Method Overriding Interview Questions — Beginner to Advanced

blocks.text: These questions are consistently asked in Java fresher and experienced-hire interviews, OCPJP/OCA certification exams, and campus placement tests covering OOP concepts.

items.q: Q1. What is method overriding in Java? How is it different from method overloading?
items.a: Method overriding occurs when a subclass provides its own implementation of a method already defined in the parent class, with the same name and same parameter list. It enables runtime polymorphism — the JVM selects the correct version at runtime based on the actual object type. Method overloading, by contrast, occurs in the same class when multiple methods share the same name but differ in parameter list (number, type, or order). Overloading is resolved at compile time (static binding), while overriding is resolved at runtime (dynamic binding). @Override applies only to overriding.

items.q: Q2. What are the rules for method overriding in Java?
items.a: The rules are: (1) Same method name and parameter list as the parent. (2) Return type must be same or covariant (subtype). (3) Access modifier cannot be more restrictive than parent. (4) Cannot throw new or broader checked exceptions than parent. (5) Cannot override static, final, or private methods. (6) Requires inheritance (IS-A relationship). (7) @Override annotation is not mandatory but strongly recommended — it lets the compiler enforce all these rules automatically.

items.q: Q3. What is Dynamic Method Dispatch in Java?
items.a: Dynamic Method Dispatch (also called runtime polymorphism) is the mechanism by which Java resolves a call to an overridden method at runtime, based on the actual type of the object the reference variable points to — not the declared type of the reference. Example: Animal a = new Dog(); a.sound(); — Java resolves sound() to Dog's version at runtime, even though the reference type is Animal. Internally, the JVM uses a virtual method table (vtable) per class to look up the correct method pointer in O(1) time.

items.q: Q4. Can we override a static method in Java?
items.a: No — static methods cannot be overridden. They belong to the class, not instances, so dynamic dispatch doesn't apply. If a subclass defines a static method with the same signature as a parent's static method, it is called method hiding — the child's method hides the parent's. The key difference: with overriding, the method called depends on the runtime object type. With hiding, it depends on the reference type at compile time. @Override on a static method causes a compile error in Java.

items.q: Q5. What is the purpose of the @Override annotation?
items.a: @Override is a compile-time annotation that tells the compiler: 'this method intends to override a method from its superclass or interface.' If the method does NOT actually override anything (wrong signature, typo, wrong parameter), the compiler immediately throws an error — preventing a silent bug where a new method is created instead of an override. It also documents intent — readers know at a glance which methods are overrides. While not required, @Override should be considered mandatory in professional Java code.

items.q: Q6. Can we override a private method in Java?
items.a: No — private methods cannot be overridden. Private methods are not inherited by subclasses — they are invisible outside their defining class. If a subclass defines a method with the same name as a parent's private method, it creates a completely new, unrelated method in the subclass. There is no runtime or compile-time connection between the two. @Override on such a method causes a compile error because there is nothing to override.

items.q: Q7. What is covariant return type in method overriding?
items.a: Covariant return type (introduced in Java 5) allows the overriding method to return a subtype of the return type declared in the parent method. Before Java 5, the return type had to be exactly the same. Example: if parent's createAnimal() returns Animal, child can override it to return Dog (since Dog extends Animal). This makes APIs cleaner — callers using a child reference get a Dog directly without casting. It is particularly useful in Builder patterns, factory methods, and fluent APIs.

items.q: Q8. What are the exception rules for method overriding?
items.a: The overriding method: (1) CAN throw no exception. (2) CAN throw the same checked exception. (3) CAN throw a narrower (subtype) checked exception. (4) CAN throw any unchecked (runtime) exception. (5) CANNOT throw a new checked exception not declared in parent. (6) CANNOT throw a broader (supertype) checked exception. These rules enforce the Liskov Substitution Principle — code relying on the parent type must be able to handle exceptions from any subtype without breaking.

items.q: Q9. If a parent class constructor calls an overridable method, what happens when the child object is created?
items.a: The child class's overridden version of the method is called BEFORE the child constructor runs — meaning the child's instance fields are still uninitialized (at default values: 0, null, false). This is because the parent constructor runs first, and at that point the object is already of the child type (dynamic dispatch applies). This commonly causes NullPointerException or logic bugs when the overridden method uses child instance fields. Rule: never call overridable methods from constructors — use final or private methods in constructors, or delegate to a post-construction init() method.

items.q: Q10. What is the difference between method hiding and method overriding in Java?
items.a: Method overriding (instance methods): the method called depends on the RUNTIME object type — dynamic dispatch. Animal a = new Dog(); a.sound() calls Dog's sound(). This is true polymorphism. Method hiding (static methods): the method called depends on the REFERENCE TYPE at COMPILE TIME — no dynamic dispatch. Animal a = new Dog(); a.staticMethod() calls Animal's static method because the reference type is Animal. Hiding is resolved statically. @Override works with overriding but causes a compile error on static methods. True polymorphism only applies to instance method overriding.

B overrides greet(), so B's version is called. This demonstrates dynamic method dispatch — the runtime type (C) determines which method is called, and since C inherits from B which has greet(), B's version runs.

This will NOT compile. Error: display() in Child cannot override display() in Parent — attempting to assign weaker access privileges (protected is more restrictive than public). Rule: the overriding method's access modifier cannot be more restrictive than the parent's. Parent's display() is public; Child's cannot be protected or package-private. Fix: change 'protected void display()' to 'public void display()' in Child.

Bug: Dog's method is MakeSound() (capital M) — not makeSound() (lowercase m). This is NOT an override — it defines a new method MakeSound() with a different name. makeSound() in Animal is NOT overridden. So a.makeSound() calls Animal's version, printing 'Generic sound' — not 'Woof' as intended. Fix: rename to makeSound() and add @Override — the annotation would have caught this at compile time had it been used. Lesson: always use @Override.

Output: Derived. This demonstrates covariant return type. Derived overrides getInstance() and returns Derived (a subtype of Base) — a valid covariant override. b is a Base reference holding a Derived object → dynamic dispatch → Derived's getInstance() runs → prints 'Derived'. The fact that the return type is narrowed to Derived does not affect the override's validity — and does not affect the call because the call is through a Base reference.

This will NOT compile. Error: action() in Child cannot override action() in Parent — overridden method does not throw Exception. Exception is a BROADER (supertype) checked exception than IOException (IOException extends Exception). Overriding methods cannot throw broader checked exceptions — this would break code that handles only IOException when using a Parent reference. Fix: Child can throw IOException (same), FileNotFoundException (narrower subtype), no exception at all, or only unchecked exceptions like RuntimeException.

Output: Parent static (line 1), Child show (line 2). Explanation: p.print() — print() is static. Static method calls are resolved by REFERENCE TYPE at compile time (method hiding). p is declared as Parent → Parent.print() is called → 'Parent static'. p.show() — show() is an instance method with override in Child. Dynamic dispatch: p holds a Child object → Child's show() is called → 'Child show'. This clearly shows the difference between method hiding (static, reference-type based) and method overriding (instance, object-type based).

Problem: Animal's constructor calls logCreation() — an overridable method. When new Dog('Rex', 'Labrador') is called: (1) super(name) runs Animal's constructor. (2) Animal's constructor calls logCreation(). (3) Dynamic dispatch invokes Dog's logCreation() — but Dog's constructor hasn't run yet! breed is still null. (4) Output: 'Dog created: breed=null' — wrong! Fix options: (a) Make logCreation() final in Animal — prevents override, uses Animal's version safely. (b) Make logCreation() private in Animal — not inheritable. (c) Remove the constructor call, let callers call logCreation() after construction. (d) Use a post-construction init() hook instead.

Define a perform() abstract method in a common Animal base class/interface, then override it in each subclass: abstract class Animal { public abstract void perform(); } / class Dog extends Animal { @Override public void perform() { fetchBall(); } } / class Cat extends Animal { @Override public void perform() { purr(); } } / class Bird extends Animal { @Override public void perform() { sing(); } }. Then: void processAnimal(Animal animal) { animal.perform(); } — one line, no instanceof, no casting, polymorphism handles dispatch automatically. Adding new animal types requires no changes to processAnimal() — it's open for extension, closed for modification (Open/Closed Principle).

sections.title: Conclusion — Method Overriding: The Engine of Runtime Polymorphism

blocks.text: Method overriding is one of the most fundamental pillars of Java's object-oriented model. It is the mechanism that brings runtime polymorphism to life — allowing you to write code that works with parent class references but automatically executes subclass-specific behaviour at runtime. Without method overriding, inheritance would merely be code reuse; with it, inheritance becomes a powerful tool for building flexible, extensible architectures.

The difference between a junior and senior Java developer is often visible in how they use overriding. Junior code skips @Override, accidentally overloads instead of overrides, calls overridable methods from constructors, and uses instanceof chains where polymorphism belongs. Senior code uses @Override religiously, leverages covariant return types for clean APIs, always overrides hashCode() with equals(), and designs class hierarchies where the instanceof antipattern never appears.

items.q: What is method overriding in Java?
items.a: Method overriding in Java is when a subclass provides a specific implementation of a method that is already defined in its parent class. The overriding method must have the same name, same parameter list, and a compatible (same or covariant) return type. It enables runtime polymorphism — the JVM decides at runtime which version of the method to call based on the actual object type, not the reference type. Overriding is the mechanism behind Dynamic Method Dispatch.

items.q: What is the difference between method overriding and method overloading in Java?
items.a: Overriding: same method name AND same parameter list, different implementation in subclass, resolved at runtime (dynamic binding), requires inheritance, enables runtime polymorphism. Overloading: same method name, different parameter list, can be in the same class, resolved at compile time (static binding), compile-time polymorphism. @Override annotation applies only to overriding. The key test: if the parameter list is different, it's overloading — not overriding.

items.q: What are the rules for method overriding in Java?
items.a: Key rules: (1) Same method name and parameter list. (2) Return type same or covariant (subtype) since Java 5. (3) Access modifier cannot be more restrictive than parent. (4) Cannot throw new or broader checked exceptions. (5) Cannot override static, final, or private methods. (6) Inheritance (IS-A) is required. (7) Always use @Override annotation so the compiler enforces all rules automatically.

items.q: What is the use of @Override annotation in Java?
items.a: @Override is a compile-time annotation that verifies the method actually overrides something in the parent class or interface. If not (due to typo, wrong parameter, etc.), the compiler throws an error immediately — preventing a silent bug where a new method is accidentally created instead of an override. It also documents intent clearly for other developers. While optional, it should be treated as mandatory in all professional Java code.

items.q: Can we override a static method in Java?
items.a: No — static methods cannot be overridden. Static methods belong to the class, not instances, so dynamic dispatch doesn't apply. Defining a static method with the same signature in a subclass is called method hiding — the subclass's method hides the parent's, but which one is called depends on the reference type at compile time, not the runtime object type. @Override on a static method causes a compile-time error in Java.
